title: Persistence: SwiftData, Core Data, Keychain & Files
scopeHtml: Scope: SwiftData, Core Data, UserDefaults, FileManager, Keychain, CloudKit sync, Room comparison, migrations.

notes.title: Baseline and the persistence map
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Android you choose between Room (SQLite), DataStore/SharedPreferences, files in filesDir, and the Keystore/EncryptedSharedPreferences for secrets. iOS has the same layers, each with a different name and different rules.

Baseline. Swift 6, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 minimum. New code uses SwiftData (iOS 17+), @Observable, async/await and actors. Core Data is shown because most shipping apps still use it ("you will meet this in old codebases"). Fast-moving or unconfirmed items are marked verify.

Android iOS
Room (@Entity, @Dao, RoomDatabase) SwiftData (@Model, ModelContext, ModelContainer) or Core Data
Room migrations (Migration(1,2)) VersionedSchema + SchemaMigrationPlan (SwiftData), mapping models (Core Data)
SharedPreferences / DataStore UserDefaults, @AppStorage
filesDir, cacheDir Application Support, Documents, Caches directories
Android Keystore / EncryptedSharedPreferences Keychain Services
Firebase sync / Drive backup CloudKit / iCloud
Flow from DAO @Query, NSFetchedResultsController, observation of @Model 
 Small flags, settings        -> UserDefaults / @AppStorage
 Secrets, tokens, passwords   -> Keychain
 Structured, queryable data   -> SwiftData / Core Data / GRDB (SQLite)
 Blobs, documents, caches     -> FileManager (Application Support / Caches / Documents)
 Cross-device sync            -> CloudKit (via SwiftData/Core Data) or your backend

Real industry examples. Apple apps (Notes, Photos) use Core Data/CloudKit; Airbnb, Instagram and many large apps use SQLite directly or via wrappers (Instagram has used custom stores; WhatsApp uses SQLite), while newer SwiftUI-first apps adopt SwiftData.

Everyday analogy. Your home: a sticky note on the fridge (UserDefaults), a safe (Keychain), a filing cabinet with an index (database), a storage box in the attic (files).

Common interview traps.

  • Using UserDefaults for tokens or large lists.
  • Assuming SwiftData is just Room: it is an object graph store with a context, closer to Hibernate/Realm than to SQL DAOs.
  • Forgetting data protection classes and backup behaviour of each location.

notes.title: SwiftData: @Model, container, context and @Query
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Room you declare @Entity, a @Dao with SQL and a RoomDatabase; you collect Flow<List<T>>. SwiftData is an object-graph persistence layer: you annotate a class with @Model, a ModelContainer owns the store, a ModelContext is the unit of work (a scratch pad of tracked objects), and @Query in a SwiftUI view is a live, auto-updating fetch. It is built on top of Core Data's storage machinery (SQLite underneath), verify internals are not public API.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import SwiftData

@Model
final class Note {
    @Attribute(.unique) var id: UUID
    var title: String
    var body: String
    var createdAt: Date
    @Relationship(deleteRule: .cascade, inverse: \Attachment.note)
    var attachments: [Attachment] = []

    init(title: String, body: String) {
        self.id = UUID()
        self.title = title
        self.body = body
        self.createdAt = .now
    }
}

@Model
final class Attachment {
    var fileName: String
    var note: Note?
    init(fileName: String) { self.fileName = fileName }
}
@Entity(tableName = "notes")
data class NoteEntity(
    @PrimaryKey val id: String,
    val title: String,
    val body: String,
    val createdAt: Long,
)

@Entity(tableName = "attachments",
    foreignKeys = [ForeignKey(NoteEntity::class, ["id"], ["noteId"], onDelete = CASCADE)])
data class AttachmentEntity(@PrimaryKey(autoGenerate = true) val id: Long = 0,
                            val noteId: String, val fileName: String)

Set up the container once at the app root and read it via the environment:

@main
struct NotesApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup { NotesList() }
            .modelContainer(for: [Note.self, Attachment.self])   // creates the SQLite store
    }
}

struct NotesList: View {
    @Environment(\.modelContext) private var context
    @Query(sort: \Note.createdAt, order: .reverse) private var notes: [Note]

    var body: some View {
        List {
            ForEach(notes) { note in Text(note.title) }
                .onDelete { idx in idx.forEach { context.delete(notes[$0]) } }
        }
        .toolbar { Button("Add") { context.insert(Note(title: "New", body: "")) } }
    }
}

Key facts:

  • @Model is a macro: it rewrites stored properties into observable computed properties backed by the model's storage and conforms the class to PersistentModel and Observable. Models must be final class types (reference semantics, like Room entities mapped to a rich object), and are NOT Sendable.
  • context.insert, mutate properties, context.delete. autosaveEnabled is true for the main context, saving at system-chosen moments (UI events); call try context.save() explicitly before critical moments (background transition, sharing data to an extension).
  • Predicates use the #Predicate macro with type-checked Swift expressions, not strings: #Predicate<Note> { $0.title.contains("swift") } (not every Swift operation is supported; unsupported closures fail at compile time or runtime, verify for complex predicates, optional chaining and enums).
  • FetchDescriptor<Note>(predicate:sortBy:) with fetchLimit, fetchOffset, propertiesToFetch for non-view code: let result = try context.fetch(descriptor).
  • Attributes: .unique (upsert-like behaviour on insert when the key matches), .externalStorage (large blobs stored as files), .encrypt (verify), .transformable, @Transient for non-persisted properties.
  • Enums and structs that are Codable can be stored as properties.

Version and caveats. SwiftData launched with iOS 17; iOS 18 added #Index, #Unique and history tracking improvements (verify). Early releases had bugs with complex migrations, relationships and background contexts; teams often wait for their minimum target to reach iOS 18 before betting on it. Check release notes for the exact fixes.

Real industry examples. Apple's WWDC sample apps; indie and mid-size SwiftUI-only apps adopt it; larger production apps with older deployment targets stay on Core Data or GRDB. Airbnb and Uber do not rely on SwiftData for core data (they use custom SQLite-based storage; verify).

Everyday analogy. The container is the whole warehouse, the context is your clipboard of changes: nothing becomes official in the warehouse until you hand the clipboard in (save).

Common interview traps.

  • Treating @Query like a Flow you can use in a ViewModel; @Query only works inside SwiftUI views. In a view model you use FetchDescriptor and manual refresh, or ModelContext notifications.
  • Sharing model objects between threads/actors: they belong to the context's actor.
  • Expecting autosave to be instant or to occur on background contexts.
  • Forgetting that modelContext.delete of a parent applies the relationship delete rule you configured.

notes.title: Concurrency with SwiftData and Core Data
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Room dispatches queries on its own executor; entities are plain data classes you can pass freely between threads. In iOS, managed objects are thread-confined and bound to their context, which is the biggest mental shift.

SwiftData: the main context is @MainActor (the modelContext environment value). For background work create a ModelActor:

@ModelActor
actor NoteImporter {
    func importNotes(_ dtos: [NoteDTO]) throws {
        for dto in dtos {
            modelContext.insert(Note(title: dto.title, body: dto.body))
        }
        try modelContext.save()
    }
}

// usage
let importer = NoteImporter(modelContainer: container)
try await importer.importNotes(dtos)

@ModelActor generates modelContainer, modelContext and an executor so the context runs on the actor's serial executor. Pass PersistentIdentifier (which is Sendable) or DTOs across actor boundaries, never model objects:

let ids: [PersistentIdentifier] = await importer.fetchIDs()
// On the main actor: let note = context.model(for: ids[0]) as? Note

Swift 6 strict checking will flag passing a @Model instance between isolation domains. Transactions in an actor are not auto-observed by the main context immediately; changes saved in the shared store propagate to the main context (merge happens when the context is saved/refreshed, verify timing on your OS target).

Core Data (legacy, but ubiquitous): rules are:

  • viewContext is main-queue; use container.performBackgroundTask { ctx in ... } or newBackgroundContext() for writes.
  • Always touch a context's objects inside its perform { } / performAndWait { } block (or await context.perform { }).
  • Set viewContext.automaticallyMergesChangesFromParent = true so background saves flow to the UI.
  • Pass NSManagedObjectID between contexts.
  • Merge policy: set NSMergeByPropertyObjectTrumpMergePolicy or you get NSMergeConflict save errors.
  • Launch-argument -com.apple.CoreData.ConcurrencyDebug 1 crashes immediately on misuse and is the standard debugging tool.

Crash signatures. "Illegal attempt to establish a relationship between objects in different contexts"; "Core Data could not fulfill a fault" (object deleted in another context); EXC_BAD_ACCESS or "Fatal error: Never access a property of a model after it has been deleted"-type messages; SwiftData "Thread/actor isolation" runtime asserts in Swift 6. They are all variants of cross-context object use.

Batch operations. Core Data NSBatchInsertRequest, NSBatchDeleteRequest, NSBatchUpdateRequest write directly to SQLite and bypass contexts, which is far faster for tens of thousands of rows but needs a manual merge of changes into live contexts (NSManagedObjectContext.mergeChanges(fromRemoteContextSave:into:)). SwiftData's equivalent is context.delete(model:where:) and batched inserts in a background actor with periodic saves.

Real examples. Apps that import large JSON payloads (Reddit clients, podcast apps like Overcast-style libraries) run the import on a background context in batches of 500 to 5,000 rows and save per batch to cap memory.

Everyday analogy. Each context is a separate notebook copy of the same ledger; you may only write in your own notebook, and you pass the account NUMBER (ID) to a colleague, not your notebook.

Common interview traps.

  • Passing NSManagedObject or @Model instances across threads.
  • Saving a huge import in one transaction and hitting a memory warning.
  • Forgetting automaticallyMergesChangesFromParent, leaving the UI stale.
  • Assuming Room-like thread safety.

notes.title: Core Data stack and why legacy apps use it
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Think of Core Data as an ORM with change tracking (Hibernate-style) rather than a thin SQL layer like Room. It predates Swift (introduced with iOS 3, 2009), so almost every large production app and many SDKs have a .xcdatamodeld file.

The stack:

 NSPersistentContainer
   |- NSManagedObjectModel          (schema from .xcdatamodeld, versions)
   |- NSPersistentStoreCoordinator  (talks to the store files)
   |     '- NSPersistentStore       (SQLite, binary, in-memory)
   '- NSManagedObjectContext        (viewContext: main queue; background contexts)
          '- NSManagedObject subclasses (your entities)
final class CoreDataStack {
    static let shared = CoreDataStack()
    let container: NSPersistentContainer

    private init() {
        container = NSPersistentContainer(name: "Model")
        container.persistentStoreDescriptions.first?
            .setOption(true as NSNumber, forKey: NSPersistentHistoryTrackingKey)
        container.loadPersistentStores { _, error in
            if let error { fatalError("Store failed: \(error)") }   // production: log + recover
        }
        container.viewContext.automaticallyMergesChangesFromParent = true
        container.viewContext.mergePolicy = NSMergeByPropertyObjectTrumpMergePolicy
    }
}

// fetch
let request = NSFetchRequest<NoteMO>(entityName: "NoteMO")
request.predicate = NSPredicate(format: "title CONTAINS[cd] %@", "swift")
request.sortDescriptors = [NSSortDescriptor(key: "createdAt", ascending: false)]
request.fetchBatchSize = 50
let notes = try context.fetch(request)

Concepts you must know:

  • Faulting. Fetched objects are lightweight "faults"; properties load from the store (or row cache) on first access. This keeps memory low and is why accessing an object whose row was deleted crashes ("could not fulfill a fault").
  • NSFetchedResultsController feeds UITableView/UICollectionView with sections and diffs, the pre-SwiftUI equivalent of PagingSource + Flow. SwiftUI uses @FetchRequest.
  • Codegen. Entity classes are either generated automatically (Class Definition) or hand-written (Manual/None). Optional/NSNumber quirks come from Objective-C heritage.
  • SQLite files. The store is Model.sqlite plus -wal and -shm files (write-ahead log). Copying only the main file while the app is running loses recent data. Use NSPersistentStoreCoordinator.migratePersistentStore or a backup-aware copy to move/export.
  • Debugging. Launch arguments -com.apple.CoreData.SQLDebug 1 log SQL, and Instruments has a Core Data template (fetches, faults, saves).

Why legacy apps use it and still choose it. Mature, deeply integrated with CloudKit (NSPersistentCloudKitContainer), battle-tested at huge scale, supports batch ops, history tracking and extensions, and works on iOS 3+ which matters for older deployment targets. SwiftData requires iOS 17+. Migrating is a risk: the store file format stays compatible (SwiftData can open a Core Data store with matching model, verify migration path), so incremental adoption is possible.

Real industry examples. Apple's own apps, Day One, Things, Bear and countless banking and retail apps; Mozilla Firefox for iOS used custom SQLite instead, and Realm's mobile database fought for the market before MongoDB sunset Atlas Device Sync/SDK maintenance (Realm SDK is deprecated direction, verify current status).

Everyday analogy. Core Data is a library with a librarian who hands you a book-shaped placeholder (fault) and fetches the real pages only when you open it.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing Core Data is a database; it is an object graph manager that can use SQLite.
  • Using viewContext for heavy writes.
  • Calling fatalError on store load failure in production (it wipes user trust; implement recovery).
  • Copying the .sqlite file without -wal.

notes.title: Schema migration in SwiftData and Core Data
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Room needs a version bump, Migration(1, 2) objects with SQL, or AutoMigration. iOS migrations are model-versioning based and declarative.

SwiftData. Define versioned schemas and a plan:

enum SchemaV1: VersionedSchema {
    static var versionIdentifier = Schema.Version(1, 0, 0)
    static var models: [any PersistentModel.Type] { [Note.self] }
    @Model final class Note { var title: String; init(title: String) { self.title = title } }
}

enum SchemaV2: VersionedSchema {
    static var versionIdentifier = Schema.Version(2, 0, 0)
    static var models: [any PersistentModel.Type] { [Note.self] }
    @Model final class Note {
        var title: String
        var isPinned: Bool = false          // new column with default: lightweight
        init(title: String) { self.title = title }
    }
}

enum NotesMigrationPlan: SchemaMigrationPlan {
    static var schemas: [any VersionedSchema.Type] { [SchemaV1.self, SchemaV2.self] }
    static var stages: [MigrationStage] {
        [.lightweight(fromVersion: SchemaV1.self, toVersion: SchemaV2.self)]
    }
}

let container = try ModelContainer(
    for: SchemaV2.Note.self,
    migrationPlan: NotesMigrationPlan.self)

A custom stage (MigrationStage.custom(fromVersion:toVersion:willMigrate:didMigrate:)) runs code before/after the structural change for data fix-ups (e.g. dedupe, split a name into first/last). Use it for renames with @Attribute(originalName: "oldName") (a lightweight rename hint) and for transformations that need data.

Best practice: keep each schema version's model classes nested in the version enum, never edit a shipped version, and test the migration with a store created by the previous release (keep a fixture .store file in the test bundle).

Core Data. Two flavours:

  • Lightweight (inferred): adding optional or defaulted attributes, removing attributes, renaming (with Renaming ID). Enable shouldMigrateStoreAutomatically and shouldInferMappingModelAutomatically (both true by default in NSPersistentContainer). Create a new model version in Xcode (Editor > Add Model Version) and mark it current.
  • Heavy-weight: an explicit .xcmappingmodel with entity/property mappings and optionally a custom NSEntityMigrationPolicy subclass for complex transformations (merging entities, splitting tables). It migrates the whole store, copying source to destination, so it needs free disk space about double the store size and can be slow; run progressive migration step by step (v1 to v2 to v3) rather than v1 to v4 directly.

Failure modes: "The model used to open the store is incompatible with the one used to create the store" (NSCocoaErrorDomain 134100) when you changed the model without versioning; a crash at launch for all upgrading users, the most expensive persistence bug there is, because it only appears for users with old data, never for fresh installs. Always test upgrade paths from every previously released version.

Recovery strategy. On migration failure: log to Sentry/Crashlytics with the error domain and code, back up the broken store, then either rebuild from the server (if the data is a cache) or surface a recovery screen. Never loop crashing on launch; add a launch-crash counter that switches to a safe mode.

Real examples. Apps with sync-from-server data (Twitter-style timelines, banking histories) often treat the local DB as a cache and delete-and-rebuild on failure; apps with user-authored content (notes, journals, finance trackers) invest in careful progressive migrations and backups.

Everyday analogy. Migration is renovating a house while the family still lives in it: small tweaks (add a shelf) need no planning; moving walls needs a written plan and a place to store the furniture.

Common interview traps.

  • Editing a shipped schema version in place.
  • Skipping the test with a real old-version store.
  • Assuming SwiftData migrations are automatic for every change; rename and type changes need plan stages.
  • Forgetting that heavy-weight migration needs lots of temporary disk space.

notes.title: UserDefaults, @AppStorage and DataStore comparison
notes.html:
Android equivalent. SharedPreferences (legacy) and Jetpack DataStore (Preferences or Proto, async, Flow-based). UserDefaults is most like SharedPreferences: key-value, synchronous API, backed by a plist file, but it is thread-safe and cached in memory and does not block on every write.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
// Direct API
UserDefaults.standard.set(true, forKey: "onboardingDone")
let done = UserDefaults.standard.bool(forKey: "onboardingDone")

// SwiftUI: reads/writes and re-renders on change
struct SettingsView: View {
    @AppStorage("darkModeOverride") private var override = false
    var body: some View { Toggle("Dark mode", isOn: $override) }
}
val Context.dataStore by preferencesDataStore("settings")
val KEY = booleanPreferencesKey("onboardingDone")
suspend fun setDone(ctx: Context) = ctx.dataStore.edit { it[KEY] = true }
val done: Flow<Boolean> = ctx.dataStore.data.map { it[KEY] ?: false }

Facts:

  • Supported value types: Bool, Int, Double, String, URL, Data, Date, and arrays/dictionaries of those (property list types). Custom types via Codable + Data/JSON, or @AppStorage with RawRepresentable (String/Int enums).
  • It is for small preferences. Everything is loaded into memory at launch; storing megabytes slows app start (Instruments' App Launch template shows plist loading).
  • Not secure or encrypted: readable in backups and on jailbroken devices. No tokens.
  • Shared storage across an app and its extensions/widgets needs an App Group: UserDefaults(suiteName: "group.com.acme.app"). Widget and Share-extension bugs are mostly "wrote to .standard instead of the suite".
  • Observation. UserDefaults.didChangeNotification or KVO on keys; @AppStorage handles it for SwiftUI. There is no Flow, but you can wrap with NotificationCenter.default.notifications(named:) as an AsyncSequence.
  • NSUbiquitousKeyValueStore syncs small key-values via iCloud (limit about 1 MB total, 1024 keys, verify).
  • Privacy manifests: since 2024 App Store submissions need PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy declaring "required reason" for UserDefaults use (reason codes such as CA92.1); missing declarations trigger App Store Connect warnings or rejection (verify current enforcement).
  • Swift 6 note: UserDefaults is Sendable (documented thread-safe, verify); @AppStorage is for views.

DataStore's differences: transactional async writes with Flow; UserDefaults gives synchronous reads, simpler but without transaction guarantees on multi-key updates. Wrapping defaults in a small SettingsStore protocol makes it testable (inject UserDefaults(suiteName: UUID().uuidString) in tests).

Real examples. Feature-flag caches, onboarding flags, last-selected-tab and sort order live in UserDefaults across Spotify-, Airbnb-style apps; remote config SDKs (Firebase Remote Config) cache in their own stores.

Everyday analogy. UserDefaults is the sticky-note board by the door: perfect for "bring umbrella", terrible for storing your passport.

Common interview traps.

  • Storing auth tokens or big lists in defaults.
  • Using .standard where an App Group suite is needed (widgets show defaults).
  • Expecting UserDefaults to throw or be async.
  • Missing the privacy manifest required-reason declaration.

notes.title: FileManager, sandbox directories and Codable to disk
notes.html:
Android equivalent. context.filesDir, cacheDir, getExternalFilesDir. iOS apps are sandboxed; each has a container whose path changes between installs, so never persist absolute paths; store file names and rebuild the URL.

Directory API Backed up to iCloud System may purge Use for
Documents .documentDirectory Yes No User-created content (visible in Files app if enabled)
Application Support .applicationSupportDirectory Yes No App data, databases (create the directory first)
Caches .cachesDirectory No Yes, under storage pressure Re-downloadable data, image cache
tmp FileManager.default.temporaryDirectory No Yes Short-lived files
App Group container containerURL(forSecurityApplicationGroupIdentifier:) Depends No Sharing with widgets/extensions 
enum Disk {
    static var support: URL {
        let url = FileManager.default.urls(for: .applicationSupportDirectory, in: .userDomainMask)[0]
        try? FileManager.default.createDirectory(at: url, withIntermediateDirectories: true)
        return url
    }

    static func save<T: Encodable>(_ value: T, as name: String) throws {
        let data = try JSONEncoder().encode(value)
        // .atomic writes to a temp file then renames: no half-written file after a crash
        try data.write(to: support.appendingPathComponent(name), options: [.atomic, .completeFileProtection])
    }

    static func load<T: Decodable>(_ type: T.Type, from name: String) throws -> T {
        let data = try Data(contentsOf: support.appendingPathComponent(name))
        return try JSONDecoder().decode(T.self, from: data)
    }
}

Facts:

  • Data Protection. .completeFileProtection encrypts the file with a key unavailable while the device is locked. Reading it from a background task while locked fails (a classic BGTask/silent-push bug). Use .completeFileProtectionUntilFirstUserAuthentication for files background code must read; it is the default for new apps' files since iOS 7+ (verify).
  • Exclude from backup. Large re-creatable files outside Caches should set URLResourceValues.isExcludedFromBackup = true, otherwise App Review and users' iCloud storage suffer.
  • Atomic writes prevent corruption on kill/crash; FileHandle or streaming for large files; Data(contentsOf:options: .mappedIfSafe) memory-maps big files.
  • File coordination. NSFileCoordinator is required for iCloud Drive/document-provider files and shared containers with concurrent writers.
  • Blocking. File I/O is synchronous; do it off the main actor in a nonisolated async function or an actor. Large reads on the main thread appear as hangs in MetricKit.
  • Android difference. There is no external storage permission model; user-visible files go through the document picker (UIDocumentPickerViewController, SwiftUI .fileImporter) with security-scoped URLs: call startAccessingSecurityScopedResource() and balance with stop....
  • Photos have their own PhotoKit library with permissions; you do not write into a public folder.

Codable to disk is perfect for small, whole-object state (a cached config, a draft). If you find yourself rewriting a 10 MB JSON file for each change, move to a database.

Real examples. Instagram- and Pinterest-style image caches sit in Caches and are purged by the OS, so the app tolerates missing files; document-centric apps (Notion offline cache, Bear) store in Application Support/App Group containers so widgets can read.

Everyday analogy. Documents is your desk drawer (kept, backed up), Caches is the recycling bin that the cleaner may empty any time.

Common interview traps.

  • Saving absolute file paths; the container UUID changes after reinstall or update (sometimes on update).
  • Putting re-downloadable data in Documents and bloating backups.
  • Reading a protected file while the device is locked.
  • Writing non-atomically then crashing, leaving a truncated file.

notes.title: Keychain for secrets
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Android Keystore generates and guards keys; you encrypt secrets with them (EncryptedSharedPreferences/Tink). The iOS Keychain is a simpler, system-level encrypted store of small secrets (passwords, tokens, keys, certificates) that the OS protects, backed by the Secure Enclave for keys on supported hardware.

The C-style API is SecItemAdd, SecItemCopyMatching, SecItemUpdate, SecItemDelete with CFDictionary queries. A minimal wrapper:

enum KeychainError: Error { case status(OSStatus) }

struct Keychain {
    let service: String   // e.g. bundle id

    func set(_ data: Data, account: String) throws {
        let query: [CFString: Any] = [
            kSecClass: kSecClassGenericPassword,
            kSecAttrService: service,
            kSecAttrAccount: account
        ]
        let attrs: [CFString: Any] = [
            kSecValueData: data,
            kSecAttrAccessible: kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly
        ]
        let status = SecItemUpdate(query as CFDictionary, attrs as CFDictionary)
        if status == errSecItemNotFound {
            let add = query.merging(attrs) { $1 }
            let s = SecItemAdd(add as CFDictionary, nil)
            guard s == errSecSuccess else { throw KeychainError.status(s) }
        } else if status != errSecSuccess {
            throw KeychainError.status(status)
        }
    }

    func get(account: String) throws -> Data? {
        let query: [CFString: Any] = [
            kSecClass: kSecClassGenericPassword,
            kSecAttrService: service,
            kSecAttrAccount: account,
            kSecReturnData: true,
            kSecMatchLimit: kSecMatchLimitOne
        ]
        var item: CFTypeRef?
        let status = SecItemCopyMatching(query as CFDictionary, &item)
        if status == errSecItemNotFound { return nil }
        guard status == errSecSuccess else { throw KeychainError.status(status) }
        return item as? Data
    }
}

Facts that distinguish seniors:

  • Accessibility classes (kSecAttrAccessible...): WhenUnlocked, AfterFirstUnlock (needed for background tasks and silent pushes), WhenPasscodeSet...ThisDeviceOnly, and ...ThisDeviceOnly variants that are excluded from backups and do not migrate to new devices. Pick AfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly for refresh tokens used in background; wrong choice = background refresh fails with errSecInteractionNotAllowed (-25308) while the phone is locked.
  • Survives app deletion? Keychain items historically persisted across uninstall/reinstall on the same device (the app sees the old token on a fresh install). Many apps store a "first launch" flag in UserDefaults and wipe stale Keychain items on first run if they want clean state. Behaviour has been stable but verify on current iOS.
  • Sharing. Keychain access groups share items between apps from the same team and with extensions (entitlement keychain-access-groups). Default group is <TeamID>.<bundle id>.
  • Biometrics. SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags with .biometryCurrentSet or .userPresence stores items that need Face ID/Touch ID to read; LocalAuthentication (LAContext) is for gating UI without storing secrets. NSFaceIDUsageDescription is required in Info.plist or Face ID use crashes/denies.
  • Simulator vs device. Keychain behaviour on Simulator differs (no real Secure Enclave). Test on devices. Unit tests need a host app or keychain-access-group entitlement, or errSecMissingEntitlement (-34018) appears, a very common CI failure.
  • Third-party wrappers: KeychainAccess, Valet (Square), SwiftKeychainWrapper. Valet adds sane accessibility defaults and shared-group support.
  • CryptoKit provides keys (SymmetricKey, SecureEnclave.P256) for encrypting larger data; store the key in the Keychain, the ciphertext in a file or database.
  • Secrets that should never ship in the binary (API keys) belong on a backend; anything you embed is extractable with strings on the IPA.

Real examples. Banking apps and 1Password, Signal store keys with ThisDeviceOnly and Secure Enclave protection; Firebase Auth stores its tokens in the Keychain by default and you can see it in the shared-group requirement for app extensions.

Everyday analogy. The Keychain is a hotel safe in the room's wall: staff (the OS) hold the master mechanism, you choose when it opens (after first unlock, only on this device).

Common interview traps.

  • Keeping tokens in UserDefaults "because Keychain is complicated".
  • Wrong accessibility class breaking background refresh.
  • Assuming Keychain data vanishes on uninstall.
  • Not handling errSecDuplicateItem (-25299) because you used Add without Update.

notes.title: CloudKit, iCloud sync and other storage options
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Firebase Firestore/Realtime DB or Google Drive App Data folder for sync. On Apple platforms the first-party answer is CloudKit with the user's iCloud account, with no server for you to run and free quotas that scale with users.

CloudKit with Core Data / SwiftData.

// Core Data
let container = NSPersistentCloudKitContainer(name: "Model")
// requires: iCloud capability + CloudKit container, Push Notifications, Background Modes (Remote notifications)
// SwiftData: automatic when the iCloud capability and a container are configured
let config = ModelConfiguration(cloudKitDatabase: .automatic)   // verify exact options on your Xcode version
let container = try ModelContainer(for: Note.self, configurations: config)

Schema restrictions when syncing with CloudKit: all attributes must be optional or have defaults, no unique constraints, relationships must be optional with inverses, no .deny delete rule. The CloudKit schema must be promoted from Development to Production in the CloudKit Dashboard BEFORE shipping, otherwise production users silently never sync, a famous launch-day bug. Schema changes after production are additive only (you cannot delete or rename fields).

How it works: Core Data mirrors changes into a CloudKit private database zone using persistent history tracking, and silent pushes (CKSubscription) wake the app to fetch changes. Sharing with other users uses CKShare (NSPersistentCloudKitContainer.share(...)). Conflicts resolve with last-writer-wins at the field/record level, so for concurrent edits plan your model (append-only logs or per-field timestamps).

Other CloudKit uses: public databases for shared content, CKQuery and CKFetchRecordZoneChangesOperation for hand-rolled sync, CKAsset for files. Users without iCloud signed in cannot sync, so check CKContainer.accountStatus() and degrade to local-only.

Other options.

  • GRDB.swift: a mature SQLite toolkit with Codable records, ValueObservation (an AsyncSequence/Combine stream of query results, the nearest equivalent of Room's Flow), migrations as ordered closures, and WAL. A favourite of teams that want SQL control and Room-like feel; GRDB works with Swift concurrency via DatabaseQueue/DatabasePool async reads and writes.
  • SQLite.swift / FMDB: thinner wrappers (FMDB is Objective-C era).
  • Realm: object database popular 2015 to 2022; MongoDB has been winding down Atlas Device Sync and signalled deprecation of the SDKs, so treat it as legacy to maintain, not for new work (verify current status).
  • SQLiteData / Point-Free's tools and swift-sharing: community options building on GRDB (verify maturity).
  • Firebase Firestore / your own backend: when sync is cross-platform (Android and iOS users on the same account), CloudKit does not reach Android (only web via CloudKit JS), so cross-platform products use their own backend.
Need Pick
Apple-only, free sync, simple model SwiftData/Core Data + CloudKit
SQL control, heavy queries, Room feel GRDB
Cross-platform account sync Own backend + local DB as cache
Legacy Realm app Keep, plan migration

Real examples. Apple Notes, Reminders, Day One and Bear sync through CloudKit; Things uses its own cloud; Notion, Slack and Figma use their own backends with local caches.

Everyday analogy. CloudKit is a shared family calendar kept by the building's concierge: free and automatic for everyone in the building, but the concierge does not serve people in other buildings (Android).

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting to deploy the CloudKit schema to Production.
  • Using unique constraints or required relationships with CloudKit-synced models.
  • Assuming CloudKit sync is real-time or conflict-free.
  • Choosing Realm for a new project without checking its roadmap.

notes.title: Production incidents, offline-first design and interview patterns
notes.html:
Incident patterns.

  • Launch crash after update. Core Data store incompatible after a model change (NSCocoaErrorDomain 134100/134110) hits only upgrading users. Defence: versioned models, upgrade tests from every released version, safe-mode recovery.
  • Main-thread hang from a fetch. context.fetch of thousands of rows in viewDidLoad or in a SwiftUI body (@Query with an expensive predicate). Fix: fetchLimit, indexes (#Index, Core Data fetch indexes), background actor, pagination.
  • Cross-context crash. NSManagedObject captured in a Task and used on another thread. Run Core Data with -com.apple.CoreData.ConcurrencyDebug 1 during QA.
  • Widget shows stale or no data. Data written to the app sandbox instead of the App Group container.
  • Keychain access in background fails. Item is WhenUnlocked, push arrives while locked.
  • Disk full. Writes fail with NSCocoaErrorDomain 640; handle by pruning caches and surfacing a message.
  • Backups bloated. Large downloaded media in Documents without isExcludedFromBackup; users complain about iCloud storage.

Offline-first pattern (Room-style repository). The database is the single source of truth, the network refreshes it, the UI observes the database:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@MainActor @Observable
final class FeedModel {
    private let repo: FeedRepository
    var items: [Post] = []
    init(repo: FeedRepository) { self.repo = repo }

    func start() async {
        // GRDB ValueObservation / SwiftData fetch stream, then refresh network in parallel
        async let refresh: Void = repo.refresh()
        for await latest in repo.postsStream() { items = latest }
        try? await refresh
    }
}
class FeedViewModel(private val repo: FeedRepository) : ViewModel() {
    val items = repo.postsFlow().stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Lazily, emptyList())
    init { viewModelScope.launch { repo.refresh() } }
}

Use DTO structs for the network, @Model/entities for storage, and plain value-type domain models for UI to avoid leaking managed objects into views and across actors; this is the same layering as Room entity, domain model, UI state.

Testing persistence. SwiftData: ModelConfiguration(isStoredInMemoryOnly: true) for a fresh container per test with Swift Testing's @Test. Core Data: NSPersistentStoreDescription with type = NSInMemoryStoreType (or /dev/null URL for SQLite semantics, which also keeps constraints and WAL behaviour). Keychain: abstract behind a protocol and use an in-memory fake; run one device test for the real class.

Privacy. Data deletion on logout must clear Keychain, defaults, database and caches. Apps that offer account deletion must remove server data too (App Store guideline 5.1.1(v)). Data Protection: mark sensitive stores completeUnlessOpen or stronger.

Rapid-fire facts for interviews.

  • Managed objects/models are context-bound; pass IDs or DTOs.
  • SwiftData needs iOS 17+, @Query only in views, @ModelActor for background work.
  • Migrations: versioned schemas, lightweight vs custom stages; always test with old store files.
  • UserDefaults is small, unencrypted, needs App Group for extensions.
  • Keychain accessibility class decides whether background code can read.
  • CloudKit schema must be deployed to Production; model constraints apply.

Real examples. Engineering blogs from apps with local-first designs (Linear, Things, Bear) describe DB-as-source-of-truth and per-change IDs for sync; Apple's NSPersistentHistoryTracking powers extension-to-app change merging.

Everyday analogy. Offline-first is a notebook you always write in; the cloud is a photocopier that syncs copies when it is available. You never wait for the photocopier to write.

Common interview traps.

  • Letting views observe the network instead of the database.
  • Leaking managed objects to the UI layer.
  • Forgetting to wipe all storage on logout.
  • Not testing migration paths.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• iOS persistence layers mirror Android's but with different names and rules: UserDefaults (SharedPreferences/DataStore), SwiftData/Core Data (Room), FileManager directories (filesDir/cacheDir), Keychain (Keystore), CloudKit (Firebase-like sync).
  • SwiftData (iOS 17+) uses @Model classes, a ModelContainer, a ModelContext unit of work and @Query in views; it is an object graph store, not a DAO/SQL layer. Mature apps still run on Core Data (container, coordinator, contexts, faults, fetch requests).
  • Model objects are context-bound and not Sendable: use @ModelActor or background contexts and pass PersistentIdentifier/NSManagedObjectID or DTOs.
  • Migrate with VersionedSchema + SchemaMigrationPlan (SwiftData) or model versions, inferred or mapping-model migration (Core Data); always test upgrading from every shipped version.
  • UserDefaults/@AppStorage is for small, non-secret preferences, needs App Groups for extensions, and requires a privacy-manifest reason declaration.
  • Pick the right sandbox directory (Documents, Application Support, Caches, tmp), save atomically, mind Data Protection levels and backup exclusion, and never store absolute paths.
  • The Keychain stores secrets; choose the accessibility class deliberately (AfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly for background-refreshed tokens), expect items to survive reinstall, and use device tests.
  • CloudKit sync needs optional-friendly schemas and a Production schema deployment; GRDB is the strong SQL option, Realm is legacy, cross-platform sync needs your own backend.
  • Design offline-first: the database is the source of truth, observed by the UI, refreshed from the network.
  • Verify before relying on: SwiftData iOS 18 additions, ModelConfiguration CloudKit options, .encrypt attribute availability, UserDefaults privacy-reason enforcement, Realm and community library status.
